hints: Look closely at the formula for citric acid and count how many acidic carboxylic acid groups it really has.
Notice there are three $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ groups, so one mole of citric acid needs three moles of $\text{NaOH}$ for full neutralisation.
Work out moles of $\text{NaOH}$ needed from 0.0050 mol of acid, then use volume equals moles divided by concentration to finish.
walkthrough:
**Find the basicity of citric acid**

Citric acid looks complicated, but focus only on the acidic protons. Carboxylic acid groups, $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$, are acidic, alcohol $\text{OH}$ groups are not.

Formula: $\text{HO}_2\text{CCH}_2\text{C(OH)(CO}_2\text{H)CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ contains three $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ groups, so it is tribasic.

**Write the mole ratio**

One mole of a tribasic acid neutralises three moles of a monobasic alkali like $\text{NaOH}$.
$$\text{citric acid} + 3\text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{sodium citrate} + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Calculate moles of NaOH needed**

Multiply the moles of acid by 3.
$$n(\text{NaOH}) = 3 \times 0.0050 = 0.015 \text{ mol}$$

**Convert moles to volume**

Use $V = n / c$ with $c = 0.40 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$.
$$V = \frac{0.015}{0.40} = 0.0375 \text{ dm}^3 = 37.5 \text{ cm}^3$$

options.A: 12.5 cm3 gives only 0.0050 mol of NaOH, a 1:1 ratio. This treats citric acid as monobasic and ignores the other two carboxylic acid groups.
options.B: 25.0 cm3 gives 0.010 mol of NaOH, a 1:2 ratio. This treats citric acid as dibasic, missing one $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ group.
options.C: 37.5 cm3 gives 0.015 mol of NaOH, exactly three times 0.0050 mol of acid. This correctly matches the three acidic $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ groups in tribasic citric acid.
options.D: 50.0 cm3 gives 0.020 mol of NaOH, a 1:4 ratio. This wrongly counts the alcoholic $\text{C(OH)}$ group as acidic, but alcohol OH does not react with NaOH under these conditions.
